title: Short Stuff: Sardines!
summary: Short Stuff episode with Josh and Chuck (Jerry sitting in for Dave) on sardines. One host discusses first trying sardines on a half bagel and finding the whole-little-fish texture off-putting while the flavor was fine. The hosts compare sardines to tuna, salmon and anchovies, and suggest frying or grilling them. They cover mercury (sardines eat plankton, so low mercury versus bioaccumulation in predatory fish), the nutritional benefits (omega-3s, calcium from edible bones, vitamin D, B12, phosphorus, selenium, protein and fat that is satiating), a side note on omega-3 supplements and atrial fibrillation risk, and cautions for people with gout, kidney stones, high blood pressure or chronic kidney disease (purines, uric acid, protein load, sodium). They advise buying sardines packed in water, note BPA and other bisphenols in canned food, and point to an earlier Short Stuff on BPA. The hosts say they are not doctors, dietitians or nutritionists.
topics: Stuff You Should Know Short Stuff

segments.title: Opening banter about sardines
segments.summary: Josh introduces the short stuff on sardines. One host reports trying sardines for the first time and finding the texture off-putting while the flavor was fine. Josh says he doesn't recall recommending them.

segments.title: Trying sardines on bagels and cooking tips
segments.summary: A host describes eating sardines on a half bagel from Essa Bagel and the feeling of the whole little fish looking back. Josh contrasts sardines with ground tuna and salmon and says the smell is stronger than the taste. The hosts say sardines taste unlike tuna and nothing like anchovies. They suggest frying or grilling them, or toasting them on bagels, to make them crisper.

segments.title: Sardine origins and mercury
segments.summary: The hosts note that sardines are small silvery fish found in shallow coastal temperate and subtropical oceans, popular in Portugal and Spain. They explain that sardines eat plankton, not other fish, so they carry little mercury. Mercury builds up through bioaccumulation in predatory fish, which is why sardines are a low-mercury choice.

segments.title: Branzino and tuna consumption limits
segments.summary: The hosts discuss eating branzino, including frozen fillets prepared in an oven or air fryer. One host warns about eating more than about one tin of tuna a week. The conversation turns to Jeremy Piven and his reported mercury poisoning from sushi, and to the film PCU.

segments.title: Nutrition: calcium, omega-3s, and bones
segments.summary: The hosts describe sardines as nutrient dense. Eating the tiny soft bones gives calcium, roughly a third of the daily need according to the US government, which helps people who are lactose intolerant. Sardines also provide vitamin D, B12, phosphorus, selenium and omega-3 fatty acids. One host says a recent meta-analysis suggests omega-3 supplements may raise atrial fibrillation risk for people with a family history of heart disease, and that he has stopped his daily supplement.

segments.title: Protein, fat, and satiety
segments.summary: The hosts say sardines have a good balance of protein and healthy fat, low in saturated fat, and enough protein to keep people full. One host likes them for light lunches.

segments.title: Sardines in Canada and gout and kidney warnings
segments.summary: The hosts joke about bringing sardines into Canada. They then say people with gout, kidney stones or high blood pressure should be careful with sardines because of purines and uric acid. The hosts repeat the moderation point.

segments.title: Chronic kidney disease, sodium, and choosing canned fish
segments.summary: The hosts say that sardines are high in protein, which can strain the kidneys in people with chronic kidney disease. They say to consult a professional and that they are not doctors, dietitians or nutritionists. Sardines can be high in sodium, so buy versions packed in water. The hosts note that water-packed tuna often gets more mayonnaise, which cancels out the benefit.

segments.title: BPA and bisphenols in cans
segments.summary: Josh says that cans may contain BPA or other bisphenols, including replacement bisphenols labeled BPA-free. He points listeners to an earlier Short Stuff episode on BPA.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck wraps up the short stuff.
